title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: From food to an absorbed molecule
text:
From food to an absorbed molecule
Ingestion brings food into the digestive system. Mechanical processing changes particle size and mixes contents. Chemical digestion uses reactions, often enzyme-catalysed hydrolysis, to make smaller molecules available for absorption. Enzymes have particular substrates and working conditions; a digestive tract contains regions with different secretions and environments. The gut lumen is continuous with the outside world. A nutrient reaches the internal environment only after crossing an absorptive barrier.
In a mammalian small intestine, folds, villi and microscopic projections on epithelial cells increase the area available for absorption. Capillaries and lymphatic routes remove absorbed materials, helping maintain transport. Carbohydrate-derived monosaccharides and amino acids commonly enter blood, while much absorbed dietary lipid is packaged and enters lymph first. These routes show why “absorption” is not one identical membrane process for every nutrient. The organs supplying secretions also matter: pancreatic enzymes and bile contribute to processing food in the intestine.
Eliminating unabsorbed material in faeces is egestion. Removing metabolic wastes produced within the animal is excretion. The distinction matters when constructing an energy budget or explaining a kidney’s function. OpenStax offers a supporting account of digestive processes.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: Digestive form follows the food problem
text:
Digestive form follows the food problem
Animal diets differ in nutrient concentration, physical structure and chemical defences. A predatory animal faces different processing demands from an animal eating fibrous plant tissue. Many animals lack enzymes that directly digest cellulose effectively. Symbiotic microbes can break down plant polymers and produce compounds the host can use. The host must provide conditions and retention time that sustain that fermentation.
In a ruminant, microbial fermentation occurs before the small intestine. Microbes and their products can then contribute to the host’s nutrition. Hindgut fermenters maintain substantial fermentation later in the tract. Where fermentation occurs changes which products are readily absorbed and whether microbial biomass reaches major sites of protein digestion. These strategies involve trade-offs in passage time, food intake and nutrient recovery; one is not universally superior for every food supply or body size.
For histology, relate an absorptive epithelium to its lumen and underlying transport tissues. Smooth muscle layers help propel contents, while glands and specialised epithelial cells contribute secretions. A diagram that labels “villus” without showing the lumen, epithelial barrier and internal removal route misses the functional explanation. The broad comparative anatomy is covered in the reading on digestive systems.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
text:
Keep energy accounting explicit
For a simplified animal over a stated interval, ingested energy is divided between material not absorbed and absorbed energy. After accounting for energy leaving in excreted products, the remaining energy can support metabolic expenditure and net storage or production. Exact ecological bookkeeping conventions vary, so define your terms before calculating. Here we use:
\[
E_{\rm ingested}=E_{\rm faeces}+E_{\rm excreted}+E_{\rm metabolic}+E_{\rm retained}.
\]
All quantities refer to the same interval. If intake is 100 kJ day⁻¹, faecal loss 25, excreted chemical energy 5 and metabolic expenditure 60 kJ day⁻¹, retained energy is 10 kJ day⁻¹. Retained energy can contribute to new tissue, reserves or reproductive products. A negative retained balance can mean the animal is drawing down stores. This arithmetic does not identify which nutrient limited growth, because energy and essential nutrient supplies are distinct.
Avoid double counting. Internal mechanical work ultimately dissipates largely as heat, so a budget that already includes it in metabolic expenditure should not add the same energy again as an independent heat cost. Also distinguish energy in joules from power, an energy rate in watts. One watt is one joule per second. A daily intake and an instantaneous metabolic power cannot be subtracted until converted to compatible units and time intervals.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: ATP supply, work and oxygen consumption
text:
ATP supply, work and oxygen consumption
ATP links fuel metabolism to processes such as transport and muscle activity. Aerobic metabolism uses oxygen in mitochondrial electron transfer and can support sustained ATP supply when fuels, oxygen delivery and waste removal are adequate. Anaerobic pathways can supply ATP without that immediate oxygen use, but their ATP yield per unit substrate and sustainable rates differ. An animal may use both during a single bout of activity. Oxygen consumption therefore provides useful information about aerobic metabolism without being a complete record of every ATP-producing process at every instant.
Imagine a supplied respirometry observation: a chamber contains 0.10 L of water, and oxygen concentration falls by 0.40 mg L⁻¹ in 10 minutes. The chamber’s oxygen loss is \(0.10\times0.40=0.040\) mg, giving an apparent rate of 0.0040 mg min⁻¹. If a comparable empty chamber loses 0.0010 mg min⁻¹, the blank-corrected animal rate is 0.0030 mg min⁻¹. The example is a calculation with supplied data, not a procedure for keeping animals in sealed containers.
Rate comparisons require the right denominator and context. Dividing by body mass produces a mass-specific rate, but does not automatically remove all effects of body size. Activity, temperature, feeding state, stress and time of day can also matter. Repeated readings from one animal do not create new independent animals. Any actual experiment must use the established approved protocol and conditions; physiological interpretation begins by understanding what the measurement system measures.

title: A2 — Nutrition, energy and temperature
section: Temperature changes both rates and costs
text:
Temperature changes both rates and costs
An ectotherm obtains much of the heat determining its body temperature from external sources. An endotherm generates substantial metabolic heat for temperature regulation. These terms concern heat sources. They are not identical to poikilothermy and homeothermy, which describe variation or relative stability of body temperature. An ectotherm can regulate temperature behaviourally, and an endotherm may allow body temperature to vary.
Temperature affects reaction rates, membranes and protein function. A rise can increase some physiological rates within a suitable range, yet eventually performance declines as other processes become limiting or damaged. A simple \(Q_{10}\) describes the rate ratio over a 10 °C interval:
\[Q_{10}=\left(\frac{R_2}{R_1}\right)^{10/(T_2-T_1)}.\]
If a rate increases from 2 to 4 units between 10 and 20 °C, \(Q_{10}=2\). It is a description over those conditions, not a universal constant or a license to extrapolate into thermal extremes. Use rates measured under comparable feeding, activity and acclimation conditions.
Endotherms face an energy cost when heat loss must be replaced. Insulation, posture, peripheral blood flow and behaviour alter heat exchange. Below a species- and condition-dependent thermoneutral range, resting metabolic heat production often rises as ambient temperature falls. Above a suitable range, cooling can become demanding; evaporation loses water. An ectotherm’s metabolic rate may rise with environmental warming over a moderate range. Thus two rising metabolic rates can reflect different mechanisms: defending body temperature in cold conditions or temperature-dependent processes in a warming body.

1.1

Answer






Ingestion: taking food into the digestive tract.
Digestion: breaking food down, mechanically and chemically (mainly by enzymatic hydrolysis), into molecules small enough to be absorbed.
Absorption: uptake of the products of digestion across the gut epithelium into the internal environment (blood or lymph).
Egestion: elimination of unabsorbed material from the gut as faeces.

Microbial fermentation

2.1
Why do most herbivorous vertebrates depend on symbiotic microbes to use plant cell walls, and which main products do the microbes supply to the host?






Answer





Vertebrates do not produce cellulase, so they cannot hydrolyse cellulose themselves. Microbes ferment the cellulose and supply short-chain (volatile) fatty acids, such as acetate, propionate and butyrate, which the host absorbs and uses as fuel. The microbes themselves are also a source of protein.





2.2
Classify each animal as a foregut fermenter or a hindgut fermenter.

cow
horse
sheep

Answer






Foregut (ruminant). b. Hindgut (caecum and colon). c. Foregut (ruminant).
Hindgut (caecum).






2.3
In which type of fermenter is microbial protein digested and absorbed in the small intestine, and why? How do rabbits recover microbial protein?






Answer





In a foregut fermenter. The fermentation chamber lies before the stomach and small intestine, so microbes washed out of it are digested in the small intestine like other food protein. In a hindgut fermenter the microbes grow after the small intestine and are mostly lost in the faeces. Rabbits recover them by caecotrophy: they eat the soft faeces produced from the caecum (coprophagy).

Answer






\(Q_{10}=(8.0/2.0)^{10/20}=4^{0.5}=2.0\).
\(4.0\times2.5=10\) units.






5.2
Match each term to its definition: ectotherm, endotherm, poikilotherm, homeotherm.

an animal whose body temperature varies with environmental temperature
an animal whose body temperature is determined mainly by external heat sources
an animal that keeps a relatively constant body temperature
an animal that warms its body mainly with its own metabolic heat







Answer






Poikilotherm. b. Ectotherm. c. Homeotherm. d. Endotherm.

Ectothermy and endothermy refer to the source of body heat; poikilothermy and homeothermy refer to how much body temperature varies.





5.3

In a resting ectotherm, metabolic rate usually rises when environmental temperature rises over a moderate range.
In a resting endotherm, metabolic rate is lowest within the thermoneutral zone.

Answer






False. Many ectotherms regulate body temperature by behaviour, such as basking, seeking shade and changing posture.
True. Body temperature follows environmental temperature, and reaction rates rise with temperature.
True.
False. \(Q_{10}\) describes only the measured temperature range. Outside it, rates level off and fall as proteins and membranes are damaged.






5.4

Answer





The thermoneutral zone; its lower boundary is the lower critical temperature. Below the lower critical temperature, metabolic rate rises as ambient temperature falls, because the animal must produce more heat (by shivering and non-shivering thermogenesis) to replace the faster heat loss and keep body temperature constant.

A snake lies on a warm rock.

Answer

Diffusion.






1.2
Dry air at sea level has a total pressure of 101.3 kPa and contains 20.9 % O₂. Calculate the partial pressure of O₂.

\(P_{\rm O_2}=0.209\times101.3\ \text{kPa}=21.2\) kPa (about 159 mmHg).

Answer





Surface 1: \(10\times4/2=20\). Surface 2: \(20\times2/4=10\). Transfer across surface 2 is half that across surface 1 (\(2\times\tfrac12/2=0.5\)).





1.4

3.1
Define partial pressure of O₂, haemoglobin saturation and O₂ content of blood, and give a unit for each.






Answer






\(P_{\rm O_2}\): the pressure exerted by O₂ (in blood, by the dissolved, unbound O₂); kPa or mmHg.
Saturation: the percentage of haemoglobin O₂-binding sites that are occupied; %.

Calculate the O₂ content at 75 % saturation.

Answer






\(150\times1.34=201\) mL O₂ L⁻¹.
\(0.75\times201=151\) mL O₂ L⁻¹.
\(75\times1.34\times0.98=98\) mL O₂ L⁻¹. Only the content differs (it is halved); \(P_{\rm O_2}\) and saturation are unchanged.






3.3
Why is the haemoglobin–O₂ dissociation curve sigmoid (S-shaped)?






Answer





Haemoglobin has four subunits that bind O₂ cooperatively: binding of O₂ to one subunit increases the O₂ affinity of the others. Affinity is therefore low at low \(P_{\rm O_2}\) and high at intermediate \(P_{\rm O_2}\), giving a steep middle part to the curve.

decreased temperature

Right; favours unloading. b. Right; favours unloading (Bohr effect).
Left; reduces unloading. d. Right; favours unloading.

A right shift means lower affinity: less O₂ is bound at a given \(P_{\rm O_2}\).

title: Animal physiology
text:
A useful study rhythm
Begin with the biological question, read the connected tutorial and sketch the mechanism. Use the slides for a short explanation or revision. Complete the exercise tasks with units and labelled arrows, then answer the quiz before opening its explanations. Revisit mistakes by repairing the mechanism rather than memorising the right option.
The numerical examples are invented for teaching and can be completed by hand or calculator. There is no required R component. Descriptive histology tasks prepare observation and reasoning; they do not replace the actual tissue collection, microscope work or anatomy practicals.
For integration, explain a whole-animal response using at least three units: how is it sensed, how do effectors change, what fuels it, and what transport, thermal and water costs follow? Continue with the plant half and practical work.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
An animal detecting food, escaping a threat or reproducing must connect information to action. Neural activity, endocrine signals and muscle do not operate as isolated topics. They link sensory input and internal state to effectors while using the transport and metabolic support developed in earlier units. This unit builds those links from membrane properties to whole-organism behaviour and reproductive regulation.
You should explain membrane potential and action potentials without confusing voltage with ion concentration; trace a chemical synapse and a reflex pathway; connect calcium, ATP and muscle force; distinguish hormone concentration from target-cell response; and explain a reproductive feedback loop. Use the slides, exercises and quiz.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Ion gradients create possibilities for electrical signals
text:
Ion gradients create possibilities for electrical signals
A membrane potential is a voltage difference across a cell membrane. Ion concentrations differ inside and outside cells, and membranes are selectively permeable. The combined electrical and chemical tendencies determine each ion’s electrochemical driving force. Resting membranes are often more permeable to some ions than others. ATP-dependent transport, including the sodium–potassium pump in many animal cells, maintains gradients that leak pathways would otherwise dissipate.
The inside of a resting neuron is commonly negative relative to the outside. This does not mean that all intracellular material is negatively charged: only a small charge separation near the membrane is needed for a voltage. Opening a channel changes permeability; the direction of ion movement depends on that ion’s electrochemical gradient. A sodium channel is not itself an ATP-driven sodium pump.
A small local electrical change may decay with distance. An action potential is regenerated when voltage-dependent channels activate in adjacent membrane. In a typical vertebrate axon, rapid sodium entry drives depolarisation and subsequent channel changes, including potassium conductance, contribute to repolarisation. Refractory properties limit immediate re-excitation and help organise propagation. Exact waveforms and ion contributions differ among cell types, so treat this as a representative mechanism, not a universal recipe for every excitable cell. The supporting reading explains neuronal communication.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: A signal can be coded without becoming a larger spike
text:
A signal can be coded without becoming a larger spike
Once threshold is reached under comparable conditions, an individual action potential is approximately stereotyped. Stronger stimulation can change firing frequency, timing and the number of recruited neurons rather than making each spike proportionately taller. A sensory neuron is also selective: receptor properties and neural pathways determine what kind of change it can encode. An electrical recording alone does not reveal the animal’s conscious experience.
At a chemical synapse, arrival of an action potential can open presynaptic calcium channels. Calcium entry promotes neurotransmitter release. Transmitter acts on postsynaptic receptors, changing the receiving cell’s activity. Effects depend on receptor type and the target cell’s conditions; the same transmitter name is not a complete explanation of excitation or inhibition.





flowchart LR
  S[Stimulus] --> R[Sensory receptor and afferent neuron]
  R --> I[Integration in neural circuit]
  I --> M[Motor neuron]
  M --> E[Muscle or other effector]
  E --> O[Response changes conditions]






This original reflex sketch shows a functional route rather than a detailed anatomical circuit. A simple reflex can operate without waiting for conscious decision, while information may also reach other brain regions. The existence of a fast local pathway does not imply that the entire nervous system has one linear input and one output. Integrating excitatory, inhibitory and modulatory signals helps make context-dependent responses possible.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Muscle converts chemical energy into force
text:
Muscle converts chemical energy into force
Skeletal muscle contains fibres with organised contractile machinery. Within sarcomeres, interactions between actin and myosin generate force through cycles requiring ATP. In skeletal muscle, calcium binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin and exposes the myosin-binding sites on actin. ATP binding permits myosin to detach; ATP hydrolysis prepares subsequent interactions. Therefore ATP is necessary for controlled cycling and relaxation as well as work.
At a vertebrate neuromuscular junction, motor-neuron signalling triggers a muscle electrical response. That response reaches internal membrane systems and promotes calcium release from intracellular stores. Calcium recovery helps end activation. The sequence connects a neural signal to a mechanical effect: it is more informative than saying “the nerve contracts the muscle”. OpenStax provides a supporting account of muscle contraction.
An isometric contraction develops force without an overall change in muscle length. Mechanical work on a load requires displacement; for a constant force aligned with movement, \(W=Fd\). A muscle can consume ATP while holding a load stationary even though the external mechanical work in that simple calculation is zero. Efficiency calculations must define which energy input and output are being compared.
Force varies with recruitment, activation timing, muscle length and loading conditions. A motor unit consists of a motor neuron and the muscle fibres it innervates. Recruiting more units can increase whole-muscle force without changing the amplitude of each axon’s action potentials. Smooth and cardiac muscle share actin–myosin interactions but differ in organisation and control. Smooth muscle is not simply skeletal muscle without visible stripes; its calcium regulation and activation patterns differ.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
text:
Nervous systems are diverse
Cnidarian nerve nets, ganglia and longitudinal nerve cords in many invertebrates, and vertebrate central/peripheral systems illustrate different organisations. Cephalisation concentrates sensory and integrating structures near a leading end in many bilaterally organised animals. These arrangements reflect body plans and behaviour, rather than a single scale of intelligence.
Sensory systems detect mechanical, chemical, light and other changes through specialised receptor processes. A receptor converts a stimulus into a cellular signal; subsequent neural pathways carry and interpret information. Adaptation of a sensory response to a continuing stimulus differs from evolutionary adaptation. Biological clocks add an internal timing component: daily rhythms can persist under constant conditions while environmental cues entrain their phase. State whether “adaptation” refers to receptor response, an individual’s adjustment or a heritable population feature.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Hormones work through responsive target cells
text:
Hormones work through responsive target cells
An endocrine hormone enters internal transport fluid and can reach distant cells. Only cells with suitable receptors and downstream machinery respond in the relevant way. Peptide hormones often signal through surface receptors; many steroid hormones act through intracellular receptors. The eventual response can involve enzyme activity, transport, gene expression or several of these together. “Hormones are always slow” is an unreliable rule: some effects appear rapidly, while others require longer changes in cellular state.
The response depends on secretion, transport, breakdown, receptor abundance and interactions with other signals. A high measured hormone concentration does not guarantee a large effect at every target. Neuroendocrine cells connect neural input to hormone release. Negative feedback can occur at several levels of a regulatory axis, allowing the state of a target process to influence upstream secretion. The reading on hormone action expands this distinction between signal and response.

title: A5 — Integration, movement and reproduction
section: Reproduction integrates timing, resources and feedback
text:
Reproduction integrates timing, resources and feedback
Reproduction includes gamete production, fertilisation, development and the allocation of parental resources. Species vary in internal/external fertilisation, sex organisation, reproductive cycles and parental investment. A mammalian endocrine example provides a concrete feedback model without representing all animals.
Hypothalamic GnRH stimulates pituitary release of gonadotropins, including LH and FSH. These act on gonadal cells involved in steroid production and gametogenesis. Gonadal signals feed back on hypothalamic/pituitary activity. The sign and timing of feedback can change: sustained high oestrogen under appropriate conditions can contribute to positive feedback leading to an LH surge and ovulation. It would be incorrect to describe the entire reproductive cycle as one unchanging negative-feedback loop. In male mammals, gonadal and other signals also provide feedback governing endocrine activity and sperm production. Consult the supporting account of hormonal reproductive control.
Energy availability, environmental timing and stress can influence reproduction. These links explain why studying reproductive organs alone is insufficient. The circulation carries signals, tissues need fuel, and neural pathways provide information about surroundings. In a seasonal breeder, a prediction about reproductive timing should therefore consider environmental cues and physiological state rather than one hormone measurement alone.

title: A5 self-check — Signalling and integration
section: 1. Does a sodium channel pump sodium against its gradient using ATP?
text:
1. Does a sodium channel pump sodium against its gradient using ATP?






Answer





No. A channel allows ions to move down their electrochemical driving force. ATP-dependent transport maintains gradients over time. Channel opening and active transport are different mechanisms.

title: A5 self-check — Signalling and integration
section: 2. How can a stronger stimulus be represented without taller action potentials?
text:
2. How can a stronger stimulus be represented without taller action potentials?






Answer





Firing frequency, timing and recruitment of additional neurons can change. Individual spikes remain approximately stereotyped under comparable conditions. Encoding depends on receptor and circuit properties.

title: A5 self-check — Signalling and integration
section: 3. What connects a presynaptic action potential to transmitter release at a typical chemical synapse?
text:
3. What connects a presynaptic action potential to transmitter release at a typical chemical synapse?






Answer





Voltage-dependent calcium entry into the presynaptic terminal promotes vesicle release. The transmitter then acts on postsynaptic receptors; the receptor and cell’s state determine the effect.

title: A5 self-check — Signalling and integration
section: 4. Does zero external work during a stationary hold imply zero ATP use?
text:
4. Does zero external work during a stationary hold imply zero ATP use?






Answer





No. With no displacement, the simple external \(Fd\) work is zero, but force maintenance and ion handling can consume ATP. Mechanical output is not the entire metabolic expenditure.

title: A5 self-check — Signalling and integration
section: 5. Must equal circulating hormone concentrations cause equal responses in all tissues?
text:
5. Must equal circulating hormone concentrations cause equal responses in all tissues?






Answer





No. Receptors, downstream pathways, hormone access, breakdown and sensitivity can differ. A signal concentration is one component of a response mechanism.

title: A5 self-check — Signalling and integration
section: 6. Is all mammalian reproductive feedback negative?
text:
6. Is all mammalian reproductive feedback negative?






Answer





No. Negative feedback contributes to regulation, but appropriate sustained oestrogen signalling can promote positive feedback before an LH surge. The sign depends on physiological context and timing; the loop is not an endlessly amplifying event.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
A small aquatic animal and a mammal must both deliver oxygen to living cells. They face the same physical need but differ in body size, body organisation, environment and activity. Explaining their differences requires more than listing organs. We need to connect a structure to a process, identify the constraint that the structure addresses, and ask what evidence supports the explanation.
After this unit, you should be able to connect cells, tissues and organ systems; explain an exchange constraint using size and distance; recognise the four primary tissue categories from described features; construct a negative-feedback explanation; and distinguish an individual’s response from evolutionary change. Use the slides, then the exercises and self-check quiz. No programming is needed.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
From cells to an organism
A cell is surrounded by a selectively permeable membrane. The membrane helps maintain differences between the cell and its surroundings. Transport proteins, metabolic reactions and signalling processes contribute to those differences. A multicellular animal adds extracellular fluid: most cells exchange with nearby interstitial fluid rather than directly with the outside environment. Blood, where present, transports materials between exchange organs and tissues. This arrangement means the circulation, respiratory surface and cell membrane are successive parts of one transport pathway.
A tissue combines cells and extracellular material in a functional arrangement. An organ contains several tissue types. In the intestine, an epithelial lining performs secretion and absorption, connective tissue supports it, smooth muscle moves its contents, and nervous tissue coordinates activity. An organ system groups interacting organs, but the boundaries of systems are teaching conveniences: digestion depends on circulation, nervous control and hormonal signals.
Draw an arrow from food in the gut to an absorbed nutrient in a muscle cell. The nutrient must cross the gut epithelium, enter a transport route and cross the muscle-cell membrane. Saying that digestion “gives the cells energy” skips these steps and also skips metabolism. Digestion releases absorbable molecules; cells subsequently transform chemical energy into ATP and other usable forms.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Why geometry matters
Transport across a surface depends on how much surface is available and how far material must move. To isolate the geometrical issue, imagine a cube with side length \(L\). Its surface area is \(6L^2\) and its volume is \(L^3\), so its surface-area-to-volume ratio is \(6/L\). The ratio has units of inverse length. For a cube of side 1 mm it is 6 mm⁻¹; for a cube of side 2 mm it is 3 mm⁻¹. Doubling length gives four times the surface but eight times the volume.
This does not mean that all large animals have low functional exchange areas. It explains why their exchange surfaces cannot simply be smooth scaled-up versions of a small body. Folding, branching and subdivision increase area; thin barriers shorten diffusion paths; bulk flow transports material across long distances. A mammal’s lungs and circulation solve different parts of the transport problem. Blood flow does not replace diffusion across the final barrier between a capillary and a tissue cell.
Diffusion over a long distance is slow. In a simple comparison with the same diffusing substance and conditions, the characteristic diffusion time grows with the square of distance. Increasing distance tenfold therefore makes this time scale roughly one hundredfold. This proportional argument explains the value of thin exchange barriers without requiring an exact diffusion coefficient. Real tissues also contain barriers, binding and flow, so the toy calculation is a mechanism-building aid rather than a complete physiological prediction.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Four tissue categories, many arrangements
For histology, start with what is visible and then make a functional inference. Epithelial tissue forms sheets and boundaries. Cells are closely associated, and one surface may face a lumen, meaning the inside space of a tube or cavity. An epithelium has an apical side and a basal side; their transport proteins and neighbours can differ. A thin single layer can support exchange, whereas several layers can provide protection. Neither function follows from thickness alone: location, junctions and specialised surfaces also matter.
Connective tissue contains cells within an extracellular matrix. The matrix may be flexible, strong, mineralised or fluid. Tendon, cartilage, bone and blood therefore differ substantially even though they belong to the same broad category. A connective-tissue description should mention matrix organisation rather than treating every pale space in a section as empty.
Muscle tissue develops force. Skeletal muscle typically has long striated fibres with multiple nuclei. Cardiac muscle has striated branching cells and specialised cell connections. Smooth muscle has spindle-shaped cells without the same visible striation pattern. These are useful recognition clues, but section angle and preparation affect appearance. Nervous tissue contains neurons and supporting glial cells. Neurons receive, integrate and transmit signals; glia contribute to the environment in which those signals operate.
In an actual section, record scale, orientation, cell shape, nuclear position, layering, matrix and lumen relationships before proposing an identity. A circular profile could be a cross-section of a tube rather than a spherical structure. An organ name without supporting features is a guess. The descriptions used in our exercises practise reasoning; they do not replace identifying the actual course specimens. OpenStax provides openly accessible examples of the four primary tissue types.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
text:
Regulated variables and negative feedback
An animal survives within ranges of temperature, fluid composition and other conditions. Homeostasis is the active maintenance of suitable internal conditions despite disturbances. It is dynamic: material and energy can enter and leave while a measured variable remains approximately stable. Stability does not mean that every organ is inactive or that every variable is constant.
A useful feedback explanation identifies a regulated variable, a disturbance, a sensor, a control process, an effector and the consequence of the response. For example, increased body temperature can be detected by thermosensory systems. Neural control changes heat-loss or heat-production processes. Those changes can oppose the original rise in temperature. In negative feedback, the response reduces the deviation that helped trigger it.
The control process is not necessarily a single anatomical “control centre”, and a target range can change with time or physiological state. Positive feedback instead amplifies a change and needs some terminating condition. It can be useful during a finite event, but it is not the standard explanation for long-term stability. Feedback terminology refers to the direction of the loop, not whether its consequences are desirable.





flowchart LR
  D[Disturbance raises body temperature] --> S[Temperature sensing]
  S --> C[Neural control]
  C --> E[Heat loss increases or heat production falls]
  E --> T[Body temperature moves towards defended range]
  T -->|Reduced deviation reduces response| S






This original functional sketch omits interacting pathways. Identify the opposing effect of the response, rather than inferring feedback merely from the diagram containing a loop.
Separate a controlled variable from an effector. In a thermal example, body temperature may be the regulated variable, while skin blood flow is one response that affects heat exchange. Observing increased blood flow does not establish that blood flow itself was the variable defended by the system. Use the homeostasis reading to compare another feedback loop with this example.

title: A1 — Organisation, diversity and regulation
section: Comparison without a ladder of “better” animals
text:
Comparison without a ladder of “better” animals
Different body plans face different constraints. A flat body can shorten distances to the environment, but it also limits possible geometry. A hard external covering can support and protect an animal while making exchange through the whole body surface more difficult. An insect’s tracheal system delivers gases through branching air-filled tubes, whereas a mammal uses blood for most oxygen delivery beyond the lung. These are alternative combinations of mechanisms, not stages on a ladder towards a mammal.
Evolutionary adaptation concerns heritable features shaped across generations. Acclimation concerns an individual’s adjustment to changed conditions, often under controlled conditions; acclimatisation is commonly used for adjustment in a natural setting. A fish changing its physiological performance after several weeks at a new temperature has not evolved during that experiment. A short-term response, such as changing ventilation within minutes, is also different from a sustained acclimatory change.
When explaining a trait, distinguish its current function from evidence about its evolutionary origin. A structure being useful does not by itself prove how it evolved. Comparisons are strongest when they connect environment, mechanism, performance and relevant evidence, while allowing for trade-offs and shared ancestry.

title: A1 self-check — Organisation and regulation
section: 1. Is glucose in the gut lumen already absorbed?
text:
1. Is glucose in the gut lumen already absorbed?






Answer





No. Absorption requires crossing the absorptive epithelium into an internal route. The lumen is continuous with the exterior; digestion and absorption are different processes.

title: A1 self-check — Organisation and regulation
section: 2. Double a cube’s side: what happens to its area-to-volume ratio?
text:
2. Double a cube’s side: what happens to its area-to-volume ratio?






Answer





Area increases fourfold and volume eightfold, so the ratio halves. Since \(A/V=6/L\), its units are inverse length. A real animal can increase functional area with folds or branching and use bulk flow over long distances.

title: A1 self-check — Organisation and regulation
section: 3. Does one layer of flat cells prove that a section is a lung?
text:
3. Does one layer of flat cells prove that a section is a lung?






Answer





No. It supports a thin epithelial arrangement compatible with exchange, but many locations contain thin epithelia. Organ identification needs surrounding architecture, scale and other features. Observe first; support the inference.

title: A1 self-check — Organisation and regulation
section: 4. Is a helpful response positive feedback?
text:
4. Is a helpful response positive feedback?






Answer





Not necessarily. Feedback sign describes whether the consequence opposes or amplifies the initial change. A response that reduces a temperature rise is negative feedback even if it is beneficial.

title: A1 self-check — Organisation and regulation
section: 5. Does a stable internal concentration mean no transport is occurring?
text:
5. Does a stable internal concentration mean no transport is occurring?






Answer





No. Inputs and outputs can balance while substantial transport and energy use continue. Homeostasis is dynamic maintenance, not universal inactivity.

title: A1 self-check — Organisation and regulation
section: 6. Has a fish evolved if its physiology changes after weeks in warmer water?
text:
6. Has a fish evolved if its physiology changes after weeks in warmer water?






Answer





That observation describes adjustment within an individual, compatible with acclimation. Demonstrating evolutionary adaptation requires evidence about heritable features and population change across generations, not just one individual’s useful response.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
A freshwater fish is surrounded by water yet must control water entry and replace ions. A marine bony fish faces the opposite tendencies: it loses water and gains salts. A terrestrial mammal can conserve water, but eliminating nitrogen and dissipating heat still create costs. This unit connects the physical tendencies of water and solutes with epithelial transport, excretory organs and whole-animal regulation.
You should become able to predict osmotic tendencies, distinguish osmotic concentration from tonicity, compare aquatic strategies, trace a nephron, calculate excretion from filtration/reabsorption/secretion, and explain how water and nitrogen balance interact. Use the slides, exercises and quiz.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Begin with a boundary and a permeability
text:
Begin with a boundary and a permeability
Water moves across a selectively permeable membrane in response to differences in water chemical potential. In an elementary osmotic comparison at equal pressure, the side containing more effectively retained solute tends to draw water from the other side. State which boundary is being considered: the skin, gill, intestinal wall, capillary wall and cell membrane are not interchangeable. Water entry into the animal and water entry into one of its cells are different questions.
Osmolarity counts osmotically active particles per litre of solution, often in osmoles L⁻¹ or milliosmoles L⁻¹. For an ideal teaching example, 0.10 mol L⁻¹ glucose contributes about 0.10 Osm L⁻¹, while 0.10 mol L⁻¹ NaCl contributes about 0.20 Osm L⁻¹ if treated as fully dissociated. Real solutions need not behave ideally. These particle counts are useful because osmosis depends on particle concentration, not simply the mass of dissolved material.
Tonicity predicts sustained effects on cell volume and depends on solutes that do not readily equilibrate across the relevant membrane. Two solutions with equal total osmolarity need not have the same effect if their solutes cross a membrane differently. Avoid treating every dissolved molecule as a permanently trapped osmotic particle. Hydrostatic pressure also matters: movement need not continue until solute concentrations are equal if an opposing pressure develops. The supporting reading introduces osmotic balance.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: A permeable surface creates a transport problem
text:
A permeable surface creates a transport problem
Respiratory surfaces must exchange gases, but permeability creates opportunities for water and ions to move as well. An animal cannot always make its surface perfectly impermeable while preserving other functions. It can instead alter surface properties, drink or stop drinking, move ions actively, and change urine volume and composition.
A typical freshwater teleost has body fluids more concentrated than the surrounding water. Water tends to enter and ions tend to be lost. It produces relatively large volumes of dilute urine and obtains ions through specialised transport processes and food. A typical marine teleost has body fluids less concentrated than seawater. It drinks seawater, absorbs water through the gut and eliminates excess salts through gill and renal processes. The two fish therefore use related epithelia to address different net challenges.
These are broad teleost examples, not descriptions of every fish. Marine elasmobranchs, such as sharks, retain organic osmolytes including urea and have a different strategy. Many marine invertebrates have total internal osmotic concentrations near those of their environment, yet may still regulate particular ions. An osmoconformer need not have every internal solute identical to seawater, and an osmoregulator need not maintain an absolutely unchanging internal concentration at every salinity. State the species and conditions before generalising.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Epithelia can move material against a tendency
text:
Epithelia can move material against a tendency
An epithelial transport cell has different membrane domains facing different fluids. ATP-driven pumps establish ion gradients. Other proteins couple a solute’s movement to those gradients; channels allow selected ions to move down electrochemical gradients. Water can follow osmotic gradients through membranes and water channels. The epithelium and its cell junctions determine which routes are available.
This polarity makes directional transport possible. A list of pumps without their locations does not explain net movement from the environment to blood. Draw both boundaries of a cell and show how each protein contributes to an overall route. Energy expenditure can occur at one step while another step is passive. “Water is actively pumped by the kidney” is therefore a poor description of water following gradients produced by solute transport.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: The nephron separates filtration from selective recovery
text:
The nephron separates filtration from selective recovery
In a mammalian kidney, blood enters a glomerular capillary network. Filtration produces fluid in the nephron that normally contains water and many small solutes but few cells and little large plasma protein. A filtered molecule has left the blood and entered the tubular lumen; it has not necessarily left the body. Much of that filtered material is subsequently returned to blood.
Reabsorption moves material from tubular fluid towards blood. Secretion moves material from blood/interstitium towards tubular fluid. Excretion is the amount finally leaving in urine. For a stated substance and time interval, use the accounting relation:
\[\text{excretion}=\text{filtered load}-\text{reabsorption}+\text{secretion}.\]
For example, a filtered load of 100 arbitrary amount units min⁻¹, reabsorption of 98 and secretion of 1 gives excretion of 3 units min⁻¹. Keep amount per time distinct from concentration. If urine concentration is 2 mmol L⁻¹ and urine flow is 0.001 L min⁻¹, excretion is 0.002 mmol min⁻¹. Concentrated urine does not alone establish a large total amount excreted.





flowchart LR
  B[Blood in glomerular capillaries] -->|Filtration| F[Fluid in nephron lumen]
  F --> T[Proximal tubule → loop → distal tubule]
  T --> C[Collecting duct]
  C --> U[Urine leaving kidney]
  T -->|Reabsorption| R[Blood around tubule]
  R -->|Secretion| T






The diagram is an original functional sketch; it does not show physical scale or every nephron connection. The collecting duct receives fluid from multiple nephrons. Use it to keep transport direction explicit while reading the account of kidneys and osmoregulatory organs.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: How can urine become more concentrated than plasma?
text:
How can urine become more concentrated than plasma?
Water reabsorption requires an osmotic driving force and a water-permeable route. In the mammalian kidney, specialised loop segments differ in water permeability and solute transport. Their arrangement, together with other transport and urea-handling processes, helps establish a medullary osmotic gradient. Blood vessels serving the medulla help preserve this organisation while supplying tissue. The collecting duct passes through that gradient.
Antidiuretic hormone, ADH or vasopressin, can increase collecting-duct water permeability. More water then leaves the tubular fluid when an appropriate gradient exists, reducing urine volume and increasing its concentration. The hormone does not manufacture water or simply “make the kidney filter less”. The full concentrating mechanism is more complex than one salt pump or one hairpin loop. Here, be able to explain differential permeability, gradient, water recovery and hormonal control before memorising segment names.
When osmotic concentration of body fluids rises, sensing and control processes can increase ADH release and promote drinking. When the disturbance is corrected, feedback reduces the response. Blood-volume/pressure signals can also influence water conservation; it is not a one-input switch. Compare this loop with A1’s temperature example. The reading on hormonal regulation provides a complementary account.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
section: Nitrogen disposal is part of the water budget
text:
Nitrogen disposal is part of the water budget
Breaking down amino acids creates nitrogen-containing waste. Ammonia can be released with relatively little conversion, but its handling requires attention to toxicity, concentration and removal. Urea costs energy to synthesise but can be retained or excreted at concentrations suitable for many animals. Uric acid can be eliminated with little water in a semi-solid form, though its production also has costs. No product is universally best: water availability, life stage, habitat and other physiological demands matter.
Terrestrial insects use Malpighian tubules and hindgut processes rather than mammalian nephrons. Many annelids and other invertebrates use different tubular excretory arrangements. Compare the tasks—removing waste, controlling ions, recovering water—before comparing anatomical names. Egestion of undigested food remains different from excretion of metabolically produced nitrogen.

title: A4 — Water, ions and excretion
text:
Read structure and behaviour together
A kidney section may contain round tubule profiles, glomeruli and blood vessels, but section angle can change apparent shape. Look for a capillary tuft within a surrounding space when identifying a renal corpuscle; look for epithelial organisation around a lumen in tubules. These descriptions are preparation for the real slide set, not proof that a particular specimen is available. Finally, connect anatomy to the environment: a water-saving animal may also change behaviour, diet, ventilation and heat exchange.

title: A4 self-check — Water and excretion

title: A4 self-check — Water and excretion
section: 1. What water tendency does a typical freshwater teleost face?
text:
1. What water tendency does a typical freshwater teleost face?






Answer





Its internal fluids are more concentrated than surrounding freshwater, so water tends to enter across permeable surfaces. Ion loss is a separate challenge. Compensation includes ion uptake and production of relatively abundant dilute urine.

title: A4 self-check — Water and excretion
section: 2. Does osmoconformity imply every internal ion equals its seawater concentration?
text:
2. Does osmoconformity imply every internal ion equals its seawater concentration?






Answer





No. Total osmotic concentration can be similar while selected ions are regulated. “Conformer” must be interpreted for the variable being compared.

title: A4 self-check — Water and excretion
section: 3. Is a filtered glucose molecule already excreted?
text:
3. Is a filtered glucose molecule already excreted?






Answer





No. It is in tubular fluid and can be reabsorbed. Excretion is the amount that finally leaves in urine. Filtration, reabsorption and secretion have different directions.

title: A4 self-check — Water and excretion
section: 4. Filtered load 10, reabsorption 7, secretion 2 mmol min⁻¹: what is excreted?
text:
4. Filtered load 10, reabsorption 7, secretion 2 mmol min⁻¹: what is excreted?






Answer





\(10-7+2=5\) mmol min⁻¹. All terms are rates of the same substance. Concentrations cannot be inserted into this balance without the appropriate flow.

title: A4 self-check — Water and excretion
section: 5. Can ADH action conserve water without creating water?
text:
5. Can ADH action conserve water without creating water?






Answer





Yes. Increased collecting-duct water permeability allows greater recovery when an appropriate medullary gradient exists. This reduces water leaving in urine; it does not add new water to the body’s total inputs.

title: A4 self-check — Water and excretion
section: 6. Is concentrated urine necessarily a larger solute loss per minute?
text:
6. Is concentrated urine necessarily a larger solute loss per minute?






Answer





No. Excretion rate is concentration × urine flow. Halving flow while doubling concentration leaves solute excretion unchanged. Always distinguish amount, concentration and amount per time.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text: A well-lit leaf exports sugar while a root consumes it. What connects the two, and why can the same leaf release CO2 in darkness? Explain energy capture, carbon fixation, transport, respiration and nutrient assimilation. Interpret a response without assuming that light is its only limitation.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: Capturing energy differs from fixing carbon
text:
Capturing energy differs from fixing carbon
Pigments in chloroplast thylakoids absorb light. Excitation reaches reaction centres, and electron transfer supports a proton electrochemical gradient. ATP synthase uses that gradient to form ATP. Water supplies electrons to photosystem II and oxygen is released; photosynthetic oxygen does not come directly from splitting CO2.
Linear electron flow supports ATP and NADPH formation. Cyclic flow can contribute additional ATP without equivalent net NADPH or oxygen production. ATP and reducing power are intermediate resources, not the final carbohydrate supply for the entire plant. Their production must be coordinated with use.
The Calvin–Benson cycle operates in the stroma. Rubisco adds CO2 to ribulose bisphosphate. Subsequent reactions use ATP and NADPH to reduce the products; some carbon becomes available for synthesis and export while the rest regenerates the acceptor. In standard cycle accounting, three fixed CO2 and nine ATP plus six NADPH support one net triose-phosphate equivalent. This does not represent every energetic cost of building a plant.
“Dark reactions” is a misleading name. These reactions do not consume photons directly, but light-dependent resources and regulation support them. Ordinary carbon fixation cannot continue indefinitely in darkness just because the cycle is described as light-independent.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Oxygenation imposes additional costs
Rubisco can react with oxygen instead of CO2. The resulting photorespiratory pathway recovers carbon while releasing some CO2 and consuming energy. It involves chloroplasts, peroxisomes and mitochondria. Photorespiration is distinct from mitochondrial respiration, even though both can contribute CO2 release. Under relevant conditions, warming and reduced internal CO2 favour a greater relative oxygenation rate.
Water stress can close stomata and reduce CO2 supply. Net uptake may decline despite bright light. Later limitations may involve metabolism or tissue damage. A lower measured rate alone cannot identify stomatal, photochemical or biochemical limitation. It is an integrated outcome requiring more evidence.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: C3, C4 and CAM change carbon delivery
text:
C3, C4 and CAM change carbon delivery
In C3 plants, initial Rubisco products are three-carbon compounds. C4 plants first capture inorganic carbon through PEP carboxylase into four-carbon compounds. In the common two-cell arrangement, these compounds release CO2 near Rubisco in bundle-sheath cells. Concentrating CO2 can suppress photorespiration but costs additional energy. Warm, bright conditions often favour this strategy; it is not universally superior.
CAM plants commonly take up CO2 at night and store carbon in organic acids, then release it for fixation during the day. Separating these steps in time can reduce water loss. Storage and rate constraints remain. C4 and CAM deliver concentrated CO2 to the Calvin–Benson cycle rather than replacing it.
Predict different evidence for each hypothesis. A nocturnal rise in acid content informs a CAM hypothesis; anatomy and gas-exchange responses inform a C4 hypothesis. A single observation may not establish the entire pathway. Some species show intermediate or flexible behaviour.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: A response curve describes a balance
text:
A response curve describes a balance
Net CO2 exchange balances uptake and release under the measurement conditions. At low light, increased irradiance can increase net uptake. The light compensation point is the condition at which uptake and release balance. At greater light, CO2 supply, biochemical capacity or another process can become limiting. Excess excitation can be dissipated protectively; damage exceeding repair can cause photoinhibition.
Imagine invented net rates of −2, 0, 6 and 9 µmol CO2 m⁻² s⁻¹ at 0, 50, 200 and 800 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹. Compensation is near the second observation. The smaller response per additional photon at high light does not prove which process limits it. Record temperature, CO2, humidity, leaf age and measurement order. Repeated conditions on one leaf are not separate independent plants.
Pigment concentration, chlorophyll fluorescence and CO2 exchange measure different properties. Fluorescence informs photochemical behaviour, whereas net gas exchange includes additional processes. A greener leaf need not have proportionally greater carbon uptake.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
section: Sources and sinks change with development
text:
Sources and sinks change with development
A source exports assimilate; a sink imports it for use or storage. A mature illuminated leaf is commonly a source and a root or developing fruit a sink. A storage organ can become a source during regrowth. These are current carbon roles rather than immutable organ identities.
Phloem loading raises solute content near a source, favouring water entry and pressure development. Unloading and carbon use at sinks help maintain a pressure difference driving bulk flow. Species differ in loading routes. Different tubes can carry assimilate in different directions, so phloem is not simply an exclusively downward counterpart to xylem.





flowchart LR
  light[Illuminated mature leaf] --> suc[Sucrose loading]
  suc --> pressure[Water entry and source pressure]
  pressure --> flow[Phloem bulk flow]
  flow --> young[Growing organs]
  flow --> store[Storage organs]
  store -->|During remobilisation| export[New source supplying growth]






This original schematic separates carbon roles from organ location. It omits many transport steps and does not imply that every species loads identically.
Starch can bridge day and night. Storage, export and growth demand are regulated together; reduced sink demand can change source activity. Transport is not independent of flowering, seed filling or senescence.

title: P3 — Light, carbon and the whole-plant budget
text:
Respiration supplies more than CO2
Glycolysis, the tricarboxylic-acid cycle and mitochondrial electron transport connect carbohydrate breakdown to ATP and metabolic intermediates. Plants respire in light and darkness. Roots use carbon for uptake, maintenance and growth; leaves also require mitochondrial function. Respiration is not merely wasteful reversal of photosynthesis.
When oxygen is restricted, oxidative ATP generation is limited. Fermentation can regenerate NAD+ and permit continued glycolysis, with much lower ATP yield than complete aerobic oxidation. Waterlogged roots can therefore develop energy and transport limitations despite well-lit leaves. Many seeds also use lipid reserves during establishment, connecting reserve mobilisation and organelle metabolism to developmental stage.
Nitrate must be reduced before incorporation into organic nitrogen. Ammonium assimilation requires carbon skeletons and energy. Nutrient supply can alter photosynthetic capacity, while carbon supply can limit nutrient assimilation. Whole-plant budgets require both sides. More nitrogen cannot necessarily compensate for inadequate light or lack of oxygen at roots.
For pathway introductions, consult light-dependent reactions and carbon fixation. The exercise and self-check connect these component processes to whole-plant explanations.

title: P3 — Carbon and metabolism self-check
section: 1. What supplies the oxygen released by oxygenic photosynthesis?
text:
1. What supplies the oxygen released by oxygenic photosynthesis?






Explanation





Water, through electron donation associated with photosystem II; it is not released directly from splitting CO2.

title: P3 — Carbon and metabolism self-check
text:
2. Why is “dark reactions” misleading?






Explanation





The Calvin–Benson cycle does not use photons directly but depends on resources and regulation coupled to light. The name does not imply nighttime operation.

title: P3 — Carbon and metabolism self-check
section: 3. Do green cells respire during the day?
text:
3. Do green cells respire during the day?






Explanation





Yes. Mitochondrial metabolism supports ATP supply and intermediates in illuminated tissues as well as non-green tissues.

title: P3 — Carbon and metabolism self-check
section: 4. Does a C4 pathway replace the Calvin–Benson cycle?
text:
4. Does a C4 pathway replace the Calvin–Benson cycle?






Explanation





No. It concentrates CO2 near Rubisco, usually using spatial separation and additional energy. CAM commonly separates initial uptake and release in time.

title: P3 — Carbon and metabolism self-check
section: 5. What does a measured net exchange of zero mean?
text:
5. What does a measured net exchange of zero mean?






Explanation





CO2 uptake and release balance under those measurement conditions. It does not mean all photosynthetic and respiratory processes have stopped.

title: P3 — Carbon and metabolism self-check
section: 6. Is a storage organ always a sink?
text:
6. Is a storage organ always a sink?






Explanation





No. It can export reserves during regrowth and function as a source. Source/sink describes current carbon balance.

title: P3 — Carbon and metabolism self-check
section: 7. Can more nitrate alone guarantee more growth?
text:
7. Can more nitrate alone guarantee more growth?






Explanation





No. Reduction and assimilation need energy and carbon skeletons, and other resources or stresses can limit growth.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text: A seed can remain dormant in apparently suitable soil. A shoot bends towards light, and a mature plant begins flowering after the season changes. Explain how perception, signalling, altered cellular activity and organ development connect. Distinguish a response from proof of its underlying mechanism.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
From stimulus to response
A signal must be detected by an appropriate receptor. Detection changes downstream activity, which can modify existing proteins, transport, metabolism or gene expression. The response depends on tissue, developmental state and other signals. A receptor is not the final response itself, and the amount of a hormone is not the only determinant of sensitivity.
Gene expression connects a shared genome to specialised behaviour. Transcription produces RNA; some RNAs support protein synthesis and others act directly. Regulatory proteins can change which genes are used and when. Changing gene expression does not require changing DNA sequence. Fast ion-channel responses can precede slower changes in organ anatomy.





flowchart LR
  cue[Environmental or internal cue] --> receptor[Perception]
  receptor --> fast[Existing protein and transport activity]
  receptor --> expr[Gene-expression changes]
  fast --> cell[Cell physiology]
  expr --> cell
  cell --> organ[Growth or developmental response]
  state[Tissue and developmental state] --> cell






This original scheme is a reasoning framework. Actual pathways have feedback, interactions and distinct timescales. Use it to locate the evidence: does an experiment measure a stimulus, an intermediate or the final phenotype?

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Hormones operate in interacting networks
Plant hormones are signalling molecules active at low concentrations. Their effects depend on production, transport, metabolism and perception. One hormone can affect several processes, and several hormones can affect one process. The following are useful entry points rather than one-to-one rules:








Signal class
Useful example
Interpretation caution




Auxin
Directional growth, root initiation and developmental patterning
Concentration, transport and tissue sensitivity matter


Cytokinins
Cell division, meristem activity and resource-related responses
Effects interact with other signals and developmental state


Gibberellins
Germination and stem elongation in appropriate contexts
Not every dwarf plant lacks gibberellin


ABA
Dormancy and water-stress responses
ABA responses include both rapid physiology and longer-term development


Ethylene
Fruit ripening in responsive species and other developmental/stress responses
Not all fruits use identical ripening regulation


Brassinosteroids
Growth and differentiation
Effects depend on interaction with other pathways


Jasmonates and salicylic acid
Defence and associated growth changes
Different attackers and conditions recruit different combinations



Memorising this table is insufficient. Explain a case as signal → cellular process → organ consequence. For example, a change in auxin distribution can produce unequal expansion across an organ. Root and shoot growth responses to the same auxin change can differ. “Auxin promotes growth” hides this important context dependence.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Light supplies information as well as energy
text:
Light supplies information as well as energy
Photoreceptors allow plants to detect spectral composition, direction and timing. Phytochromes respond to red/far-red light, while blue-light receptors include cryptochromes and phototropins. These signals influence developmental choices beyond photosynthetic energy supply. A seedling can change form after a small informative light exposure without obtaining much fixed carbon from it.
Red/far-red balance can provide information about neighbouring vegetation. A shoot may respond with altered elongation and resource allocation. This can improve access to light but can also increase vulnerability or reduce investment elsewhere. A response is conditional, not evidence that plants predict an intentional goal.
Phototropism involves directional light perception and differential growth. Gravitropism involves gravity perception, signal redistribution and asymmetric responses. Gravitational orientation and light direction are different cues; an experimental design must separate them before assigning a mechanism. Rotating a pot changes several physical relationships and requires controls.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Germination depends on state and conditions
text:
Germination depends on state and conditions
Imbibition restores hydration, and metabolism resumes as conditions permit. Reserve mobilisation supports the developing seedling. Radicle emergence is a commonly used operational measure of germination, but later establishment requires further growth and resource acquisition.
Dormancy means a viable seed does not germinate despite otherwise suitable conditions. Quiescence reflects unsuitable external conditions such as insufficient water. Dormancy can involve embryo state, surrounding tissues and signal balance. ABA and gibberellin pathways provide a useful model of interacting regulation, but species differ in requirements for temperature, light or other cues.
A germination percentage needs a clear denominator and time. Twelve germinated seeds out of twenty by day five gives 60%, not proof that eight are dead. They could germinate later, be dormant, or be non-viable. Independent dishes or pots matter when environmental treatment is shared. Twenty seeds in one dish do not automatically give twenty independent temperature treatments.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Vegetative growth combines production and allocation
text:
Vegetative growth combines production and allocation
Meristems generate organs while expansion changes their dimensions. Hormones, nutrients, carbon status and environment coordinate these processes. Apical dominance illustrates integration: shoot-tip activity influences lateral bud outgrowth through several interacting signals and resource relations. Removing an apex changes more than one hormone concentration and creates a wound. An altered branching pattern alone cannot identify the complete mechanism.
Secondary growth increases girth through lateral meristems. Cambial activity must be coordinated with transport and support as the shoot enlarges. Seasonal activity can alter xylem properties. A ring or tissue pattern records growth, but interpreting it requires knowledge of species and environmental history.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
section: Flowering connects leaves and the shoot apex
text:
Flowering connects leaves and the shoot apex
Plants integrate age, resource status, temperature and light timing. Photoperiodic plants measure the length of the uninterrupted night: a short-day plant flowers when the night exceeds a critical length, and a brief light break in the middle of the night prevents it. Vernalisation refers to promotion of flowering competence by extended cold in responsive plants. It is different from a universal direct trigger that makes every cold-treated plant flower immediately.
In Arabidopsis, FT provides an example of a mobile signal linking leaves with the shoot apex. Experiments expressing tagged FT and using grafts supported protein movement contributing to floral induction. This is evidence for a particular mechanism in a model system, not proof that all flowering control is identical. See the primary study by Corbesier and colleagues.
At the apex, altered gene activity changes meristem identity and organ development. Flower induction, formation of floral organs, gametophyte development, pollination, fertilisation and fruit development are distinct steps. Failure at one step need not mean that flowering was not induced.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Reproduction links generations
In flowering plants, pollen delivers sperm cells to the female gametophyte. Double fertilisation produces a zygote and endosperm, with the latter supporting seed development in an appropriate species-specific pattern. Embryogenesis establishes the next plant’s body organisation. Fruit derives from maternal tissue and can assist protection and dispersal; a seed and a fruit are not equivalent structures.
Developing seeds and fruits draw resources as sinks. Carbon limitation, water stress or temperature can affect reproductive success after a normal-looking flower forms. Measure seed number, viability or yield separately from flower number when those are the actual biological goals.

title: P4 — Signals, growth and reproduction
text:
Senescence can redistribute resources
Senescence is a regulated developmental process that can mobilise nutrients from ageing tissues. Programmed cell death participates in development and defence, but it should not be treated as synonymous with every senescence stage or every form of accidental injury. A yellowing leaf may reflect normal ageing, deficiency, stress or several processes. Tissue age and environmental controls are needed to distinguish explanations.
For an accessible introduction to light and hormone responses, consult OpenStax plant sensory systems. Work through the exercise and self-check before the final unit connects these signals to stress and applications.

No. Existing protein activity and gene-expression changes can alter physiology without changing sequence.

No. Effects depend on dose, tissue, development, sensitivity, transport and interactions with other pathways.

text:
3. How does dormancy differ from quiescence?






Explanation





A dormant viable seed fails to germinate despite otherwise suitable conditions; quiescence reflects unsuitable external conditions.

4. What is 18 germinated seeds out of 24?

75%, at the specified observation time. The remaining six are not necessarily dead.

6. Do equal flower numbers establish equal reproductive success?

No. Pollination, fertilisation, seed development and viability can differ after flowers form.

7. Is every yellow leaf proof of programmed senescence?

No. Deficiency, injury and other stress can produce yellowing. Time course, context and physiological evidence are needed.

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
text: The questions follow the tutorial and slides. Answer each question before opening its answer.

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
text:
Cell compartments

1.1
Match each structure to its main function.




Structure




A
Plasma membrane


B
Primary cell wall


C
Tonoplast


D
Chloroplast


E
Mitochondrion



Functions: (1) membrane surrounding the central vacuole; (2) site of photosynthesis; (3) selective control of exchange between the cytoplasm and the outside of the cell; (4) site of aerobic respiration; (5) resists deformation and constrains the direction of expansion.






Answer





A–3, B–5, C–1, D–2, E–4.





1.2
Define turgor pressure and state what happens to a non-woody shoot when turgor falls.






Answer





Turgor pressure is the positive hydrostatic pressure of the cell contents against the cell wall, produced when water enters a cell with a resisting wall. When turgor falls, the cells lose rigidity and the shoot wilts, even though the cells may still be alive.





1.3
Name three functions of the large central vacuole of a mature plant cell.






Answer





Any three of: storage of solutes (ions, sugars, organic acids, pigments, defensive compounds); generation of turgor by solute accumulation and water uptake; regulation of cytoplasmic pH; degradation of cellular material; allowing the cell to enlarge without making a corresponding volume of cytoplasm.





1.4
True or false? Correct any false statements.

All plastids are chloroplasts.
Leaf cells respire only in darkness.
The cell wall is selectively permeable and controls which solutes enter the cell.
Many root cells lack photosynthetically active chloroplasts.







Answer






False. Chloroplasts are one type of plastid; others include amyloplasts (starch storage) and chromoplasts (pigments).
False. Mitochondrial respiration continues in light and darkness.
False. Water and small solutes pass through the wall; selective control is exercised by the plasma membrane.
True.

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
section: Cell walls, growth and cell connections
text:
Cell walls, growth and cell connections

2.1
Name the main load-bearing component of the primary cell wall and the polymer that reinforces secondary walls of xylem conduits.






Answer





Cellulose microfibrils (embedded in a matrix of hemicelluloses, pectins and proteins). Secondary walls of xylem conduits are reinforced by lignin.





2.2
Turgor pressure is present, but a cell does not enlarge irreversibly. Name the wall property that must change to allow growth, and the two materials that must be supplied as the cell enlarges.






Answer





The wall must be loosened so that it yields (extends irreversibly) under turgor. New wall material and new plasma membrane must be supplied.





2.3
Define apoplast, symplast and plasmodesma.






Answer






Apoplast: the continuous system of cell walls and extracellular spaces outside the plasma membranes (including the lumens of dead xylem conduits).
Symplast: the cytoplasm of cells connected through plasmodesmata.
Plasmodesma: a membrane-lined channel through the cell wall that connects the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.






2.4
A solute moves from the apoplast into the symplast. Which structure must it cross?






Answer





The plasma membrane of a cell.

3.5
Give the order in which CO₂ passes these leaf structures on its way from the atmosphere to the site of fixation: mesophyll cell, stomatal pore, chloroplast stroma, intercellular air space, plasma membrane.






Answer





Stomatal pore → intercellular air space → plasma membrane → mesophyll cell (cytosol) → chloroplast stroma. CO₂ dissolves in the water of the wet cell wall before crossing the plasma membrane.





3.6
Why does opening the stomata increase both CO₂ uptake and water loss?






Answer





CO₂ diffuses in and water vapour diffuses out through the same pore. The cuticle is nearly impermeable to both, so opening the pore raises the conductance for both gases at once.

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
text:
Meristems and growth

4.1
Name the meristem responsible for each of the following.

Increase in length of a root
Production of secondary xylem and secondary phloem
Production of the protective outer bark tissue (periderm)
Regrowth of a grass leaf after its tip has been cut







Answer






Root apical meristem. b. Vascular cambium (secondary xylem inward, secondary phloem outward). c. Cork cambium (phellogen). d. Intercalary (basal) meristem.






4.2
A root segment contains 100 cells arranged end to end. Ignore spaces between cells.

Calculate the segment length in mm when the mean cell length is 40 µm.
With no cell division, the mean cell length becomes 70 µm. Calculate the new segment length and the increase.
How many 40 µm cells would give the same final length as in (b)?







Answer






100 × 40 µm = 4000 µm = 4 mm.
100 × 70 µm = 7000 µm = 7 mm; increase = 3 mm.
7000 µm / 40 µm = 175 cells. The same length can result from cell expansion or from cell division, so length alone does not identify the process.






4.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Cell differentiation requires a change in the DNA sequence.
Primary growth increases the length of roots and shoots.
Every mature plant cell can regenerate a whole plant under any conditions.







Answer






False. Differentiation results from differences in gene expression; the DNA sequence is unchanged.
True.
False. Some cells can resume division and regenerate, but this depends on genotype, developmental state and culture conditions.

title: P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant
text:
Three genomes

5.1
Name the three genomes of a plant cell and state which one encodes most of the proteins that function inside chloroplasts.






Answer





Nuclear, plastid (chloroplast) and mitochondrial genomes. Most chloroplast proteins are encoded in the nucleus, synthesised in the cytosol and imported into the chloroplast.





5.2
A mutation in a nuclear gene encoding a chloroplast-imported protein reduces photosynthesis, while the chloroplast DNA is unchanged. Is this possible? Explain in one sentence.






Answer





Yes. The protein functions in the chloroplast but its gene is in the nucleus, so a nuclear mutation can impair chloroplast function.





5.3
Leaf and root cells of one plant have the same nuclear genome but different functions. What is the reason?






Answer





They express different sets of genes (tissue-specific gene expression).
