title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Abiotic stress

1.1
For each stress, name the main physiological problem it causes.



Stress
Main problem




Drought



Salinity



Heat



Freezing










Answer












Stress
Main problem




Drought
Low soil water potential; reduced water uptake and loss of turgor


Salinity
Osmotic effect (low soil water potential) plus ion toxicity, mainly from Na⁺ and Cl⁻


Heat
Protein denaturation and increased membrane fluidity


Freezing
Ice formation in extracellular spaces dehydrates cells; ice crystals can damage membranes








1.2
Which hormone accumulates in leaves during drought, and what is its main immediate effect?






Answer





Abscisic acid (ABA). It causes stomatal closure, which reduces transpiration.





1.3
What is the cost to the plant of the response in 1.2?






Answer





Closed stomata also reduce CO₂ uptake, so photosynthesis falls. Less transpiration also means less evaporative cooling, so leaf temperature rises.





1.4
Name two kinds of compatible solutes, and explain how accumulating them helps a plant under drought or salinity.






Answer





Examples are proline, glycine betaine and sugars or sugar alcohols such as sucrose and mannitol. They lower the cell’s solute potential, so the cell can keep taking up water from a soil with low water potential. They do so without inhibiting enzymes.





1.5
Name two classes of proteins induced by heat or drought stress that help protect cells.






Answer





Heat shock proteins (chaperones that refold or stabilise proteins) and dehydrins/LEA (late embryogenesis abundant) proteins. Antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase and catalase are also accepted.





1.6
Reactive oxygen species (ROS) can damage cells. Name one other role they play in plants.






Answer





Signalling. For example, ROS act in stress signalling, stomatal closure and defence against pathogens.





1.7
Classify each as acclimation or evolutionary adaptation.

Plants of a species become more freezing-tolerant after two weeks at 4 °C.
A population on saline coastal soil has heritably higher salt tolerance than inland populations grown under the same conditions.







Answer






Acclimation (cold acclimation). b. Evolutionary adaptation.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Biotic stress and defence

2.1
Name two constitutive (pre-existing) defences and two induced defences of plants.






Answer





Constitutive: the cuticle, cell walls, thorns or trichomes, and stored specialised metabolites. Induced: callose deposition, phytoalexin production, proteinase inhibitors, and the hypersensitive response.





2.2
Match each attacker to the main defence hormone pathway: salicylic acid (SA) or jasmonic acid (JA).

A biotrophic pathogen that feeds on living tissue
A chewing caterpillar
A necrotrophic fungus that kills tissue before feeding on it







Answer






SA. b. JA. c. JA, together with ethylene. The SA and JA pathways often act antagonistically.






2.3
What is the hypersensitive response, and why is it effective against biotrophic pathogens?






Answer





It is rapid, localised death of the plant cells at the infection site. A biotrophic pathogen needs living host cells, so killing the infected cells deprives it of nutrients and limits its spread.





2.4
What is systemic acquired resistance (SAR), and which hormone is required for it?






Answer





SAR is long-lasting, broad-spectrum resistance in uninfected parts of the plant after a local infection. It requires salicylic acid.





2.5
Name the three major classes of plant specialised (secondary) metabolites, and give one example of each.






Answer






Terpenoids, e.g. pyrethrins, essential oils such as menthol, or carotenoids.
Phenolics, e.g. flavonoids, tannins or lignin.
Nitrogen-containing compounds, e.g. alkaloids such as nicotine, caffeine or morphine, and cyanogenic glycosides.






2.6
Why are many defence compounds stored as inactive precursors, such as glucosinolates or cyanogenic glycosides?






Answer





The active compound is toxic to the plant itself. The precursor is stored separately from the activating enzyme, and they meet only when tissue is damaged by a herbivore. The toxin is therefore released only at the site of attack.





2.7
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Defence compounds use carbon and nitrogen that could otherwise be used for growth.
A plant with constitutively activated jasmonate signalling grows larger than a wild-type plant.
Natural plant compounds are harmless to humans.







Answer






True. This is the basis of the growth–defence trade-off.
False. Constitutive defence activation usually reduces growth.
False. Many, such as nicotine, ricin or cyanogenic glycosides, are toxic.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Model systems

3.1
Give three properties that make Arabidopsis thaliana a useful model plant.






Answer





Any three of: a short life cycle (about 6–8 weeks); small size; a small, fully sequenced genome; self-pollination; many seeds; easy transformation with Agrobacterium (floral dip); large collections of mutants.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Transformation and tissue culture

4.1
Put the steps of Agrobacterium-mediated transformation in order.

Regenerate whole plants from the transformed cells
Insert the gene of interest into the T-DNA of a binary vector
Select transformed cells on medium containing an antibiotic or herbicide
Co-cultivate plant explants with Agrobacterium
Confirm the insertion and expression of the transgene







Answer





b → d → c → a → e.





4.2
What is a selectable marker gene? Give an example.






Answer





It is a gene, transferred together with the gene of interest, that allows only transformed cells to survive on a selective medium. Examples are nptII (kanamycin resistance), hpt (hygromycin resistance) and bar (resistance to the herbicide glufosinate).





4.3
What is the difference between stable transformation and transient expression?






Answer





In stable transformation, the transgene is integrated into the plant genome and inherited by the offspring. In transient expression, the introduced DNA is expressed for a few days without integration and is not inherited.





4.4
Name a method for delivering DNA into plant cells that does not use Agrobacterium.






Answer





Particle bombardment (biolistics). Protoplast transformation, using polyethylene glycol or electroporation, is also accepted.





4.5
What property of plant cells makes it possible to regenerate a whole plant from a single transformed cell?






Answer





Totipotency: many differentiated plant cells can dedifferentiate and regenerate all the organs of a whole plant.





4.6
In tissue culture, what does an explant form at each auxin-to-cytokinin ratio?

High auxin : cytokinin
Intermediate (roughly balanced)
Low auxin : cytokinin (high cytokinin)







Answer






Roots. b. Undifferentiated callus. c. Shoots. The exact concentrations depend on species and tissue.






4.7
Why must several independent transgenic lines be analysed, rather than one?






Answer





The T-DNA inserts at a random position in the genome. It can disrupt or activate a native gene, and tissue culture can itself cause mutations (somaclonal variation). A phenotype seen consistently in independent lines is more likely to be caused by the transgene.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Promoters and reporters

5.1
Match each promoter type to its expression pattern.







Promoter
Pattern




a. Constitutive (e.g. CaMV 35S)
1. Expressed only after exposure to a signal


b. Tissue-specific
2. Expressed in nearly all tissues at all times


c. Inducible
3. Expressed only in particular cell types, e.g. guard cells









Answer





a–2, b–3, c–1.





5.2
Name two reporter genes used in plants, and how each one is detected.






Answer






GUS (β-glucuronidase): a blue product after staining with X-Gluc.
GFP (green fluorescent protein): fluorescence under blue/UV light.
Luciferase: light emission when luciferin is supplied.

title: P5 exercises — Stress, defence and biotechnology
text:
Genetically modified crops

6.1
Match each GM trait to the gene or mechanism used.







Trait
Gene or mechanism




a. Insect resistance
1. Bacterial EPSP synthase insensitive to glyphosate


b. Herbicide tolerance
2. Carotenoid biosynthesis genes in the endosperm


c. Golden Rice
3. Cry toxin gene from Bacillus thuringiensis









Answer





a–3, b–1, c–2. Golden Rice makes β-carotene (provitamin A) in the grain.





6.2
How does the Bt (Cry) protein kill insect larvae, and why is it harmless to mammals?






Answer





In the alkaline gut of susceptible larvae, the protoxin is activated by proteases. It binds to specific receptors on the gut epithelium and forms pores, so the gut cells lyse. Mammals have an acidic stomach and lack these receptors.





6.3
What is a refuge strategy in Bt crop cultivation, and what problem does it delay?






Answer





Non-Bt plants are grown next to the Bt crop. Susceptible insects survive on the refuge and mate with any resistant insects, which keeps the resistance alleles rare. This delays the evolution of Bt resistance in the pest.





6.4
How does genome editing with CRISPR–Cas9 differ from classical transgenesis?






Answer





Classical transgenesis inserts foreign DNA into the genome. CRISPR–Cas9 makes a targeted cut in an existing gene, which can create a small mutation in that gene. The Cas9 construct can then be removed by crossing, so the final plant may contain no foreign DNA.





6.5
Classify each question as empirical (it can be answered by measurement) or value-based.

Does pollen from a GM crop reach a wild relative 100 m away?
How much uncertainty about environmental effects is acceptable?
Does a Bt crop reduce insecticide use in a region?
Who should decide whether a GM crop is grown?







Answer






Empirical. b. Value-based. c. Empirical. d. Value-based.

1.1
Define water potential (Ψ), state its usual unit in plant physiology, and give the water potential of pure water at atmospheric pressure.






Answer





Water potential is the chemical potential (free energy per unit volume) of water relative to that of pure water at atmospheric pressure and the same temperature. It is expressed in megapascals (MPa). Pure water at atmospheric pressure has Ψ = 0 MPa.





1.2
Arrange from the highest to the lowest water potential: −0.8 MPa, 0 MPa, −1.5 MPa, −0.2 MPa. In which direction does water move passively?






Answer





0 > −0.2 > −0.8 > −1.5 MPa. Water moves passively from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential.

NaCl gives two particles, so c = 0.2 osmol L⁻¹ and Ψs = −0.50 MPa.

A flaccid cell (Ψp = 0) has Ψs = −0.6 MPa. Assume the cell volume, and hence Ψs, does not change.

What is its Ψ?
It is placed in pure water. What are Ψ and Ψp at equilibrium?

From the root cell into the soil. Saline soil can therefore cause water stress although it is wet.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Uptake by roots

2.1
Name the three routes by which water crosses the root cortex and state which structure each route passes through.






Answer






Apoplastic: through cell walls and intercellular spaces, without crossing membranes.
Symplastic: from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata.
Transmembrane (transcellular): across the plasma membrane (and tonoplast) of each successive cell.






2.2

In which cell layer is the Casparian strip found?
Which compounds make it?
What is its function?







Answer






The endodermis, in the radial and transverse walls.
Suberin (with lignin).
It blocks the apoplastic route into the stele, so water and solutes must cross a plasma membrane, which allows selective uptake.






2.3
True or false? Correct any false statements.

Aquaporins pump water into root cells using ATP.
The plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase uses ATP to build an electrochemical proton gradient.
A proton-coupled carrier can move a nutrient ion against its own concentration gradient.
Inhibiting the H⁺-ATPase directly stops passive water flow through aquaporins.







Answer






False. Aquaporins are channels that increase membrane permeability to water; water moves passively down its potential gradient.
True.
True. Energy comes from protons moving down their electrochemical gradient (secondary active transport).
False. It reduces proton-coupled solute uptake; water flow through aquaporins is passive and not directly driven by ATP.






2.4
Waterlogged soil contains plenty of water, yet mineral uptake by roots falls. Give the chain of causes.






Answer





Water fills the soil pores → little O₂ reaches the roots → aerobic respiration falls → less ATP → H⁺-ATPase activity and the proton gradient decline → less active (proton-coupled) uptake of mineral ions.

3.1

water vapour diffuses out through the stomatal pore
water crosses the root endodermis
water evaporates from mesophyll cell walls into the air spaces
water enters the root from the soil
water moves up the xylem under tension







Answer





d → b → e → c → a.





3.2
Match each term to its definition: cohesion, adhesion, tension, cavitation.

Negative hydrostatic pressure in the xylem water
Attraction between water molecules through hydrogen bonding
Breakage of the water column and formation of a gas bubble in a conduit
Attraction between water molecules and the conduit walls







Answer





Cohesion–2, adhesion–4, tension–1, cavitation–3. A gas-filled conduit after cavitation is said to be embolised.





3.3
Typical water potentials in a transpiring plant are listed. Arrange them in the order water passes and state what drives the flow.
Leaf cells: −0.8 MPa. Soil: −0.1 MPa. Atmosphere (50 % relative humidity): −95 MPa. Root xylem: −0.4 MPa.

Soil (−0.1) → root xylem (−0.4) → leaf cells (−0.8) → atmosphere (−95 MPa). Water moves passively down this gradient of decreasing water potential. The energy comes from evaporation at the leaf (ultimately solar energy); the plant does not pump water.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Stomata

4.1
Put the steps of light-induced stomatal opening in order:

guard-cell water potential falls
blue light activates the guard-cell plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPase
turgor rises and the guard cells bow apart, opening the pore
K⁺ enters through inward-rectifying channels, with Cl⁻ uptake and malate synthesis
the membrane hyperpolarises
water enters the guard cells







Answer





b → e → d → a → f → c.





4.2
State whether each condition causes stomata to open or close.

Blue light at dawn
High intercellular CO₂ concentration
Increased ABA in the leaf
Low intercellular CO₂ concentration
Low leaf water potential (drought)







Answer






Open. b. Close. c. Close. d. Open. e. Close.






4.3
How does abscisic acid (ABA) close stomata? Give the sequence from ABA perception to pore closure.






Answer





ABA binds receptors in the guard cells → anion channels open and anions leave → the membrane depolarises → K⁺ leaves through outward-rectifying channels → guard-cell Ψs and Ψ rise → water leaves → turgor falls → the pore closes. ABA acts as a signal; it does not plug the pore.

title: P2 exercises — Water, minerals and transport
text:
Mineral nutrition

5.1
Define an essential element.






Answer





An element without which the plant cannot complete its life cycle, or which is part of an essential molecule or structure of the plant; its function cannot be replaced by another element.





5.2
Classify each element as a macronutrient or a micronutrient: N, Fe, K, Zn, Mg, Mo, P, Mn, S, Cu, Ca, B.






Answer





Macronutrients: N, K, Mg, P, S, Ca. Micronutrients: Fe, Zn, Mo, Mn, Cu, B. The classification refers to the amount required, not to importance.





5.3
Match each element to one role.




Element




A
Nitrogen


B
Phosphorus


C
Potassium


D
Magnesium


E
Iron



Roles: (1) central atom of chlorophyll; (2) main cation for osmotic regulation, e.g. in guard cells; (3) component of amino acids, proteins and nucleotides; (4) component of cytochromes and Fe–S proteins in electron transport; (5) component of ATP, nucleic acids and phospholipids.






Answer





A–3, B–5, C–2, D–1, E–4.





5.4
Deficiency of nitrogen first causes yellowing of the older leaves, whereas iron deficiency first causes yellowing of the young leaves. Explain the difference.






Answer





Nitrogen is mobile in the phloem: it is remobilised from old leaves to new growth, so old leaves show symptoms first. Iron is relatively immobile and cannot be withdrawn from old leaves, so new leaves, which depend on current uptake, show symptoms first.





5.5
What does each partner gain in an arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis?






Answer





The plant gains mineral nutrients, especially phosphate, and water taken up by the fungal hyphae from a larger soil volume. The fungus gains carbon (sugars and lipids) from the plant.

section: Why can wet salty soil be difficult?

Why can wet salty soil be difficult?
Water access depends on potential, pathways and regulation.
Wetness alone is insufficient.

Direction uses total potential
Water tends from higher to lower Ψ.
−0.2 MPa is higher than −0.8 MPa.

State the approximation
For the small cell examples: Ψ = Ψs + Ψp.
Gravity and matric effects matter in other settings.

title: P2 — Water and nutrition

Work one cell
Ψs = −0.9 MPa; Ψp = +0.4 MPa.
Total = −0.5 MPa. Water initially enters from surroundings at −0.2 MPa.

Routes and barriers
Apoplast, symplast and transmembrane movement.
The endodermal barrier restricts an unrestricted wall-space route into the stele.

title: P2 — Water and nutrition

Transport energy
ATP-driven proton pumps establish gradients.
Coupled carriers can use them. Aquaporins alter permeability, not passive direction.

title: P2 — Water and nutrition

Cohesion and tension
Evaporation links leaf water to negative pressure in xylem.
Conduit structure matters; embolism can disrupt transport.

title: P2 — Water and nutrition

Stomatal regulation
Guard-cell transport → water movement/turgor → pore change.
CO2 access and vapour loss share a pathway.

title: P2 — Water and nutrition

ABA is a signal
Drought responses include channel regulation and later changes.
A hormone is not a physical pore plug.

title: P2 — Water and nutrition

Essential minerals
Required amounts differ from importance.
Symptoms depend on mobility, age, roots, pH and other stresses.

Measure the right loss
Pot mass loss = soil evaporation + plant water loss + other changes.
Controls and units determine interpretation.

title: Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function
text:
A reproducible observation record
For each case record: the features explicitly supplied; the most defensible tissue class; two features supporting it; a likely function; one plausible alternative; and an observation that would discriminate between the two. Keep observation separate from inference. “Several layers of cells” is an observation; “protects against abrasion” is a functional interpretation. Do not infer a named organ from a common epithelial shape alone.

Station 1: interfaces
Case A: a continuous lining appears one cell thick. Cells are flattened, and nuclei interrupt an otherwise thin barrier. A capillary is immediately adjacent; no thick keratin layer is described.
Case B: a lining contains several cell layers. Surface cells are flattened. Deeper cells appear less flattened. The tissue borders a surface exposed to friction.
Case C: a tubular profile has a single layer of approximately cube-shaped cells around a lumen. Nuclei are central. Other sections show many similar tubules, but no specialised border can be resolved.

Classify the epithelia by layer number and surface-cell shape.
Explain why A is compatible with exchange and B with protection. Do not claim every thin lining has the same transport properties.
Could C establish “kidney” on its own? Name an additional contextual feature you would ask to inspect.







Hint





“Simple” and “stratified” describe layers; “squamous”, “cuboidal” and “columnar” describe cell shape. Function also depends on junctions, membrane proteins and the surrounding structures.





Station 2: force and information
Case D: long parallel fibres show repeated transverse bands. Multiple nuclei lie near fibre edges; fibres are not described as branching.
Case E: short branching fibres show transverse bands and central nuclei. Distinct cell-to-cell junction regions are visible.
Case F: spindle-shaped cells each have a central nucleus. No transverse bands are visible; bundles surround a hollow organ.
Case G: large cell bodies contain prominent nuclei and several processes; many smaller supporting cells surround them. The description alone does not specify which processes are axons or dendrites.

Identify the best broad tissue interpretation for each case, explaining the features rather than matching a keyword.
Which two cases are striated? Why is “striated means skeletal” insufficient?
Predict consequences of disrupting coordinated contraction in E and sustained contraction in F. Link the prediction to organ function, not diagnosis of a disease.



Station 3: organ architecture
Sketch a cross-section of a generic transport tube with an inner lining, connective support and a muscular layer. Label the lumen and identify which side contacts the transported material. Explain how a change in muscular diameter can alter flow. Then explain why a tube described this way cannot be identified confidently as either a blood vessel or a gut segment without further observations.
Draw a fish gill lamella and a mammalian alveolar interface as conceptual diagrams, not replicas of slides. Mark the environmental medium, a thin exchange barrier and blood. Write two common exchange requirements and one important difference in ventilation or medium. A functional resemblance does not establish the same evolutionary origin of every component.

title: Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function
section: Turning descriptions into genuine visual practice
text:
Turning descriptions into genuine visual practice
Use the institution’s provided normal-tissue slides when available. For each unknown, begin at low magnification, orient the tissue, then inspect selected features at higher magnification under the local microscope instructions. Record image/slide ID, magnification or scale bar, orientation and two diagnostic observations. Distinguish sectioning angle from biological shape: a longitudinal tube and its cross-section can look very different.
Do not invent a scale or copy an atlas label onto an uncertain feature. Return to the specimen if two alternatives fit. A descriptive record with justified uncertainty is better evidence than a confident name without observations.

title: Practical: evidence for tissue identity and function
text:
Completion check
Leave with the seven case records, two conceptual exchange diagrams and a paragraph answering: “What extra evidence would I need before identifying an unknown organ?” End by naming the visual skill this text exercise cannot verify. Review representative tissue images through the linked learning resources or the course atlas; no image-reuse rights are implied here.






Self-check





A: simple squamous; B: stratified squamous; C: simple cuboidal. D: skeletal muscle; E: cardiac muscle; F: smooth muscle; G: nervous tissue. C’s shape alone cannot establish a kidney origin. The diagrams should show thin barriers and large exchange area, while distinguishing water passing gills from air ventilating lungs. These answers do not replace visual specimen assessment.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
text:
Do supplied height measurements support a difference in growth between watering treatments, and what physiological explanations remain possible? This practical uses simulated growth data with the data dictionary. It can be completed with paper and a calculator. These are invented observations, not evidence about an actual species, watering recommendation or live experiment.
Twelve plants in separate pots were allocated randomly, six per treatment, after baseline height measurement. Watering is applied individually; pots are interspersed in a common growth space with positions balanced. The same plant is measured seven days later. Assume the defined treatments are the intended difference; real experiments would need records of watering doses, soil moisture, environment, handling and compliance.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
text:
Do supplied height measurements support a difference in growth between watering treatments, and what physiological explanations remain possible? Assume the defined treatments are the intended difference; real experiments would need records of watering doses, soil moisture, environment, handling and compliance.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
section: Growth is a change, not a final size
text:
Growth is a change, not a final size
Calculate height increment as final minus initial height, in mm. A taller plant at the end may have started taller; that is why baseline measurements matter. Here the table permits a within-plant change, followed by a comparison of those changes between independent treatment groups. It is not a paired comparison between a watered plant and an unrelated reduced-water plant.
G01 changes from 30 to 48 mm, an 18 mm increment over seven days. Its average height-increment rate is \(18/7=2.57\) mm day⁻¹. This average is not proof of constant daily growth: two observations cannot reveal a detailed growth trajectory.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
text:
Analysis tasks

Check the identifiers, group counts and measurement units. Count the independent pots. Explain why the baseline and final readings do not double that count.
Calculate each plant’s increment and mean daily rate. Check G07 explicitly.
Plot the individual increments by group and calculate group means and ranges. Describe the difference as reduced-water minus watered.
Calculate the relative reduction compared with the watered mean. Explain the difference between a reduction of 8 mm and a reduction of 40%.
Write a short interpretation using the terms observation, explanation and limitation accurately. No significance test is required.







Hint





G07 starts at 31 mm and ends at 41 mm, giving 10 mm rather than 41 mm growth. The denominator for relative reduction is the reference group’s mean increment, not its final mean height.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
section: Mechanisms: what could connect water supply to height?
text:
Mechanisms: what could connect water supply to height?
Plant expansion depends on cell-wall properties and water relations; cell production and developmental allocation also influence organ growth. Reduced water availability may alter turgor, stomatal conductance, carbon acquisition and hormonal signalling. These are candidate connections to the observed response, not mechanisms established by measuring height alone.

Draw two distinct causal pathways from reduced watering to lower height increment: one involving cell expansion/water status and one involving gas exchange or carbon supply. Mark which variables this dataset actually measures and which would need new observations.
A student says “shorter plants have less auxin, so the hormone caused this”. Explain the unsupported steps. How could hormone sensitivity or spatial distribution complicate an interpretation based on one hormone measurement?
Propose one non-destructive follow-up observation for each pathway and state what result would be consistent with it. A consistent result is not necessarily exclusive evidence; name an alternative explanation.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
section: Development and stress must be distinguished
text:
Development and stress must be distinguished
Plants may alter allocation, leaf area, root growth or the timing of development under changed conditions. A lower height increment is not always equivalent to lower total biomass, lower survival or a failed adaptation. Conversely, surviving while ceasing growth does not establish that a crop maintains yield. The outcome used to define “tolerance” must be explicit.
Design a follow-up comparison of two hypothetical genotypes under watered and reduced-water conditions. Draw the four genotype × treatment groups. Specify independent pots, allocation across positions, a relevant outcome and the same measurement time. Do not place all genotype 1 plants in one cabinet and genotype 2 plants in another. Keep the treatment contrast available within each genotype and the genotype contrast within each treatment.

title: Practical: growth under reduced watering
text:
Reporting and completion check
Submit the increment table, observation plot, mean comparison, two mechanism diagrams and a follow-up design. In the discussion distinguish the strong claim supported by this constructed example—different height increments under its stipulated conditions—from broader untested claims about drought resistance, carbon balance, hormones or field performance.






Numerical check





Watered increments are 18, 20, 22, 19, 21 and 20 mm, mean 20 and range 18–22. Reduced-water increments are 10, 12, 14, 11, 13 and 12 mm, mean 12 and range 10–14. Reduced-water minus watered is −8 mm; the relative reduction is 40%. Mean daily rates are about 2.86 and 1.71 mm day⁻¹. The constructed table has six independent pots per treatment.



Continue to scientific reporting or return to the practical route.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text: Could altering stomatal development help a crop conserve water without losing carbon gain, and what evidence would justify using such a plant? This activity connects anatomy, water relations, photosynthesis, genetics and ethics. It does not ask for a general vote for or against all genetically modified plants. Prepare independently, discuss in a group, then give a short individual presentation.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text: Could altering stomatal development help a crop conserve water without losing carbon gain, and what evidence would justify using such a plant? This activity connects anatomy, water relations, photosynthesis, genetics and ethics. It does not ask for a general vote for or against all genetically modified plants. Prepare independently, discuss in a group, then give a short individual presentation.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Sources to read
Use the original article by Karavolias and colleagues (2023), “Paralog editing tunes rice stomatal density to maintain photosynthesis and improve drought tolerance,” Plant Physiology 192, 1168–1182, DOI 10.1093/plphys/kiad183. The open full text includes methods, figures and limitations. The PubMed record gives bibliographic details. Read the abstract and introduction, then focus on stomatal density, gas exchange and water conservation. Inspect figure legends and relevant methods; do not rely on the abstract alone.
For broader context use National Academies (2016), Genetically Engineered Crops: Experiences and Prospects, summary. This is an evidence synthesis, not a second primary experiment. It supports discussion of different kinds of evidence and societal questions. It is not a statement of current local law; regulatory decisions require current official information and are outside this exercise.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Vocabulary bridge
A paralog is a member of a gene family arising through duplication. Related genes need not have identical expression or effects. A knockout disrupts gene function. Stomatal density counts stomata per surface area; stomatal aperture describes individual pore openings. Both can affect conductance, so fewer stomata do not automatically predict a proportional fall in measured gas exchange.
The research compares edited rice lines with a reference background, using anatomical and physiological measurements. Connect a developmental change with functional evidence while checking trade-offs and experimental scope. Do not assume a greenhouse result establishes performance in every farming environment.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Individual evidence sheet
Choose one figure comparing gas exchange and one comparing water conservation or performance. Record actual figure/panel identifiers from the article. For each, answer in your own words:

What question does this comparison address, and what is the outcome variable?
Which lines/conditions are compared? What reference is appropriate?
What do the axes and units mean? What does one point represent?
How does the caption define sample size and error bars? Does a repeated measurement create a new independent plant?
What pattern is supported? Use a numerical value only if its source and precision are clear; do not guess exact values from a small image.
Which proposed mechanism is directly measured, and which is inferred?
What would challenge an overly broad claim that fewer stomata always improve performance?

Trace one result to its methods. Record whether measurements were made in a greenhouse, chamber or field and whether the same conditions apply to every result. If a detail cannot be located, say so and identify where you looked. Resolve uncertainty rather than inventing a number.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
section: Group discussion: three kinds of question
text:
Group discussion: three kinds of question
Physiological: Can a developmental manipulation conserve water while maintaining gas exchange under the conditions tested? Explain a mechanism and possible trade-offs involving cooling, carbon supply or changing light.
Evidential: What tests are needed for a different cultivar, soil, climate, drought regime or field setting? Water conservation is not automatically a yield benefit. Describe one follow-up comparison with a relevant reference, independent units and a clear outcome.
Ethical and societal: Who might benefit, bear costs or make decisions? Consider access to seed, affordability, farmer choice, local priorities, environmental effects and alternatives such as breeding or management. Distinguish empirical claims needing data from value judgments about what should be prioritised. A possible benefit does not erase a possible risk; a possible risk does not establish that it occurs.
Each group writes a decision scenario with an explicit context—for example, a proposed locally evaluated drought-response cultivar—and lists the evidence it would request. Do not claim the article proves a particular product is currently approved or commercially available.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Individual presentation
Prepare a five-minute presentation plus two minutes of questions. This timing is a teaching suggestion, not a formal examination rule. Use up to five slides or an equivalent spoken explanation:

The physiological problem and the stomatal trade-off.
The developmental intervention and comparison design.
One anatomical finding and one physiological result.
Limits, an alternative explanation or a needed follow-up.
A conclusion separating evidence from ethical priorities.

Cite the original article and synthesis. If showing a figure, check its licence and attribution requirements; a reference alone is not permission to reuse every element. Alternatively, draw your own conceptual diagram and describe findings orally. Questions should probe reasoning, not demand memorisation of every molecular detail.

title: Practical: evaluate evidence and present a biotechnology case
text:
Feedback and completion
Listeners record one well-supported claim, one scope limit and one question. Then write a 150-word revision explaining how feedback clarifies your conclusion. Keep the evidence sheet, sources, presentation and revision. Feedback should address reasoning, source use and physiological accuracy, not require a preferred political position.
Return to the practical route.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
text:
How does moving air relate to water loss from a hypothetical plant setup? This classroom practical uses the plant-water CSV and data dictionary. No plant manipulation or apparatus procedure is required. Use the course’s actual laboratory protocol for any future measurements.
Eight independently potted plants are randomised to still or moving air, four per group. Each pot receives its setting independently; temperature, humidity, illumination and position are controlled or balanced. Soil surfaces are covered. Matched plant-free covered setups lose 0.10 g during the interval. Assume that background applies to each experimental setup. These are supplied simplifications, not observations you should claim to have verified.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
section: From a balance reading to a physiological quantity
text:
From a balance reading to a physiological quantity
An initial-to-final mass difference is a whole-setup measurement. In this exercise we attribute corrected mass loss primarily to transpired water. This is an approximation: real mass balances also require attention to leaks, soil evaporation, material added/removed and other fluxes. A balance does not measure a stomatal aperture or distinguish stomatal from cuticular water loss.
Calculate:
\[
\Delta m_{corrected}=m_{initial}-m_{final}-\Delta m_{blank}
\]
\[
E_{area}=\frac{1000\,\Delta m_{corrected}}{A\,(t/60)}.
\]
The mass values are in g, \(A\) is the stated one-sided leaf area in cm², and \(t\) is in min. The result is mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. One-sided area is a measurement convention; state it consistently rather than switching to two-sided area midway through a comparison.

Worked check
W01 loses 0.80 g. After a 0.10 g background correction, 0.70 g = 700 mg is attributed to the plant. Its area is 50 cm² and the interval 0.5 h. The area-specific loss is \(700/(50\times0.5)=28\) mg cm⁻² h⁻¹. The correction is subtracted once per setup, not once per leaf.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
text:
Tasks

Identify the experimental unit, allocation groups and number of independent replicates. Why would one shared still-air cabinet and one shared moving-air cabinet weaken a treatment comparison?
Calculate corrected water loss and area-specific rate for all eight pots. Check W06 by hand before summarising the groups.
Draw an observation plot and calculate group means. Describe the size and variation of the difference in the given units.
Draw the path from soil water through root, xylem, leaf air spaces and stomata to the atmosphere. Mark where vapour diffusion occurs.
Explain how moving air can change the boundary layer at the leaf surface. Why might stomatal regulation prevent a simple proportional response to wind speed in a real plant?
Decide whether the data establish stomatal opening, photosynthetic rate or a species’ drought tolerance. Explain what further measurements each claim would need.







Hint





W06’s observed 2.0 g loss becomes 1.9 g after correction, then 1900 mg. Divide by 25 cm² h, not by 1500 cm² min while labelling the answer per hour.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
section: Water potential: use the sign, not just the magnitude
text:
Water potential: use the sign, not just the magnitude
For a short cell-level comparison neglect gravity and matric components and use \(\Psi_w=\Psi_s+\Psi_p\). A cell has solute potential −0.8 MPa and pressure potential +0.3 MPa, so its water potential is −0.5 MPa. The adjacent solution has water potential −0.2 MPa. Predict the initial direction of net water movement across a permeable membrane, assuming the relevant solutes do not freely cross. Explain why the movement slows as cell state changes.
Then consider an adjacent solution at −0.9 MPa. The direction reverses: water moves from the higher water potential (less negative value) toward the lower water potential. The two cases do not allow you to compute a flux without hydraulic conductance, area and other information. Do not equate a potential difference in MPa with a mass-loss rate.

title: Practical: water loss, leaf area and a mass balance
text:
Completion check
Submit a labelled water-path diagram, a worked W06 calculation, the eight rates and group means, and an interpretation linking gas exchange and water conservation. Include one design limitation and your water-potential predictions.






Self-check





Still-air rates: 28, 36, 44 and 36 mg cm⁻² h⁻¹; moving-air rates: 60, 76, 92 and 76. Means are 36 and 76, a difference of 40. The cell in −0.2 MPa solution initially gains water; in −0.9 MPa solution it loses water. More water loss alone does not establish greater carbon gain or drought tolerance.



For background, read the water-potential and transpiration sections in OpenStax: transport of water and solutes. Return to the practical route.
